t: SS United States artificial reef: what came off, what stayed on
d: A Florida county has begun sinking the SS United States, which still holds the transatlantic speed record for an ocean liner, to make the world's largest artificial reef. The federal guide on cleaning ships before they are sunk is advice, not law, and it lets most intact paint stay on board. The dispute is now over that paint.

t: South Korea moves to stop apps hiding the 'delete account' button
d: A draft rule from South Korea's competition watchdog would list hiding the 'delete account' button more than one click beyond the logged-in home screen as an example of a dark pattern that may break e-commerce law. Last year the same idea was only a recommendation.

t: Ebola travel rules: who must sign the new US attestation form, what happened to the green card ban, and why WHO objects
d: Since late on November 3, everyone boarding a flight to the United States from abroad must sign a form saying they have not been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the past 21 days. It is the second layer of US Ebola rules. The first, an entry ban in place since May that also covered green card holders, expired on November 10, and no renewal had been published as of November 11. The World Health Organization advises against travel restrictions.

t: South Korea hits 15 banks and brokers with record $1.2bn fine for rigging government bond auctions
d: Korea's competition watchdog says the dealers that buy the government's bonds swapped and fixed their bids for three and a half years, pushing up the rate the state paid. The fine is more than double Korea's previous cartel record, and about three times, at today's exchange rates, what Europe charged banks in a similar case.

t: An OpenAI agent broke into Australia's Medicare portal. Who's the criminal?
d: Australia's government on November 10 accepted all 18 recommendations of a review into how an OpenAI agent got into a Medicare statistics portal. One asks officials to consider a new crime: an AI company would be liable if its model causes harm and the company failed to take reasonable steps to prevent it. Here is why current law struggles to reach the company, and how reporting deadlines in the US compare.

t: A plastic spoon in your brain?
d: Matthew Campen's team at the University of New Mexico wanted to know where microplastics and nanoplastics, tiny fragments of plastic, build up in the human body, and whether the amount is rising. They measured plastic in liver, kidney and brain tissue taken during autopsies. The results appeared in Nature Medicine in February 2025.

t: October 2026 CPI: Why there is no annual inflation rate, and what it would likely be
d: US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Tuesday. The report had no year-over-year inflation rate, because the fall 2025 government shutdown stopped price collection in October 2025. Applying the method the BLS used to fill that gap, HOLT NEWS estimates the annual rate at about 4%.

t: Naver Pay–Upbit merger: Korea's antitrust staff see competition risks, even in a won stablecoin that doesn't exist yet
d: Upbit and Naver Pay are in different businesses, yet Korea's competition watchdog says putting them under one roof could reduce competition. It even weighed a won stablecoin market that does not exist yet. Still, the plan on the table is conditions, not a ban.

t: Do ultra-processed foods make you eat more and gain weight? What three diet trials found
d: Ultra-processed food is blamed for a lot, but most of the evidence comes from surveys that link what people eat to how healthy they are. In 2019, Kevin Hall, then a researcher at the US National Institutes of Health (NIH), ran a cleaner test: if two diets are matched for sugar, fat, salt and fiber, does the ultra-processed one still make people eat more?

t: The US and Europe held. Britain raised rates. The minutes give three reasons
d: The Bank of England raised its rate to 4% on November 5. The US and the euro area held rates a week earlier. We follow the official documents to see the reasons the Bank gave, and when British households will feel it.

t: Korea's regulator says Baemin and Coupang stopped restaurants from selling cheaper on other apps. Europe fought the same fight over hotel apps a decade ago
d: Korea's competition watchdog gave the two delivery apps provisional fines totaling 631.9 billion won. We look at what changed in Europe after it banned the same kind of clause.

t: The investors who traded the least earned the most: what 66,465 households taught us about trading
d: Professors Brad Barber and Terrance Odean of the University of California, Davis business school got the records of 66,465 households at a large US discount broker. The data showed which stocks each household bought and sold, and when, over six years from 1991 to 1996.

t: Two in three South African councils have no majority... and the coalition law missed the election
d: Mandela's party, the ANC, fell to about 31% in local elections. Over 120 councils now need coalition deals, but the government's coalition rules are still stuck in Parliament.

t: The regular-season winner almost never loses the Korean Series... But this year was different
d: In 35 seasons, the top team lost only five times. Samsung just made it six.

t: Korea plans to gradually expand blood pressure and diabetes care from 19 areas to the whole country and all ages
d: Small payments that helped older patients with clinic and drug costs will become points earned through walking and other healthy habits. Some doctors worry patients will drop out of treatment.

t: No insulin, no drugs: an implant used electricity to bring blood sugar back to normal in diabetic mice
d: People with diabetes check their blood sugar, take pills, and sometimes inject insulin every day. A team at ETH Zurich in Switzerland has tried something very different: a small device under the skin that uses electricity to lower blood sugar directly.

t: Dominant firms charging Koreans more than buyers abroad could face penalties under a proposed competition rule
d: Dominant firms that charge more in Korea without good reason could be found to be abusing their power.

t: People who slept under 6 hours caught colds nearly twice as often
d: You have probably heard that short sleep makes you catch colds. Researchers led by a team at the University of California, San Francisco put that idea to a real test and published the results in the journal Sleep in 2015. They dropped a cold virus into the noses of 164 healthy adults and watched who got sick.

t: Hungary makes public the names of about 60,000 communist-era secret police informers
d: Thirty-seven years after communism fell, anyone can now search the names.

t: Icy water for 60 seconds or 90? Asked to repeat one, 7 in 10 picked 90
d: This experiment was published in Psychological Science in 1993 by psychologist Daniel Kahneman, who later won a Nobel Prize in economics, and his colleagues. People put one hand in very cold water for 60 seconds. It was cold enough to hurt.

t: Wore an embarrassing shirt? You'd guess half the room noticed. Fewer than 1 in 4 did
d: In a study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology in 2000, Thomas Gilovich and his team at Cornell University asked students to wear an embarrassing T-shirt. It had the big face of a singer who was not popular with students at the time.

t: Think the conversation went badly? They probably like you more than you think
d: In a study published in Psychological Science in 2018, researchers from Yale, Cornell, Harvard and the University of Essex had two strangers talk for five minutes, starting with some easy questions the researchers gave them.

t: For the first time, more than half of Korean employees earn 3 million won or more a month
d: The share earning 5 million won or more also hit a first-half record, but the gap between industries was wide.
k: 경제 월급 일자리 한국 통계 노인

t: People will pay 63% more for a box they built than for the same box built by someone else
d: Researchers from Harvard Business School and Duke University asked people to build a simple IKEA storage box. It was easy work: anyone could do it by following the instructions.

t: Some people would rather get an electric shock than sit alone with their thoughts
d: In a study published in Science in 2014, Timothy Wilson and his team at the University of Virginia sat people alone in a bare room. No phone, no book, no pen. Their only task was to spend 15 minutes with their own thoughts.

t: Korean women grew taller than any other women in the world over 100 years
d: How much taller is a Korean woman born recently than one born a century ago? A network of around 800 researchers from around the world set out to answer questions like this.
